title: Visualisation: 'Goldbach comet' analogue — scatter f(p) vs p coloured by p mod 840 and by Legendre profile
connection: The Goldbach comet's bands revealed the singular series' dependence on small prime factors of n; an ES comet (f(p)/log²p vs p, coloured by residues/Legendre symbols) might show bands indicating which local data govern f(p).
why: Cheap, often revealing; the repo likely has f(p) data to 10⁸ already.
first_step: Plot; look for bands; if bands exist, regress f(p)/log²p on the band variable.

title: Visualisation: Ulam-spiral / Klauber-triangle plot of C-form C_min(p) and Type I d_min(p) to spot quadratic-polynomial alignments
connection: Ulam spirals make polynomial families visible as lines; plotting the certificate parameters (or their absence) on a spiral could reveal that exceptions (409, 577, 5569, 9601, 2521) lie on a quadratic curve.
why: Five exceptions is few, but the plot costs nothing and polynomial alignment would be a strong hint toward a Mordell–Schinzel-compatible structure (identities in t with p = Q(t)).
first_step: Generate the plots for p ≤ 10⁶ with colour = log C_min; eyeball; test the exceptional primes against small quadratics.

title: Möbius inversion on the divisor lattice (Rota) for the certificate indicator: express 1[∃ a | N, a ≡ −1 (m)] via Möbius function of the lattice of divisors
connection: The event 'some divisor lies in a class' is a union over divisors; inclusion–exclusion on the divisor lattice gives an exact alternating formula; the 'Möbius algebra' of the divisor poset might simplify when the class condition is a character condition.
why: Exact combinatorial formula alternative to the character-sum formula; may expose cancellation structure.
first_step: Write the formula for N squarefree with ω factors (2^ω terms) and compare its complexity to the character formula (φ(m) terms); use whichever is smaller per regime.
refs: Rota, 'On the foundations of combinatorial theory I'

title: Numeration systems: Ostrowski numeration (based on the CF of a fixed irrational) and Zeckendorf — is there a numeration system in which 'n has an ES certificate' is a digit condition?
connection: Automatic-sequence-style question in a non-standard numeration: some sets defined by CF data (e.g. Beatty sequences) are recognisable in Ostrowski numeration (Hieronymi–Terry). ES₅ is a CF condition on a p-tied rational; maybe recognisable in a suitable numeration, making Walnut-style decision procedures applicable to sub-statements.
why: Long shot; but Ostrowski-automatic sets are a modern decidable class that includes CF-defined sets.
first_step: Read Hieronymi–Terry 'Ostrowski numeration systems, addition, and finite automata'; check if 'CF length of r(p) ≤ 3' can be phrased for p in a fixed Ostrowski system.
refs: Hieronymi–Terry, Notre Dame J. Formal Logic 2018

title: Sturmian words / Beatty sequences: the set of x with ⌊4x/p⌋ jumps, and the 'three-gap theorem' as a structure on candidate denominators
connection: The first denominator x in 4/p = 1/x + … must satisfy p/4 < x ≤ 3p/4 (for 3 terms); the candidate set and the remainders (4x − p)/(px) are governed by the Beatty-like sequence ⌊4x/p⌋; the three-gap theorem (Steinhaus) describes gap structures of such sequences — possibly organising the 'which x leaves a two-term remainder' question.
why: Structural organisation of the x-search; cheap.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁴, mark the x in (p/4, 3p/4] whose remainder is a two-term Egyptian fraction; study the gap distribution between marked x vs three-gap predictions.

title: Collatz analogy: 'stopping time' of a certificate search as a function of p vs Collatz stopping times — both have log-ish expected values with no pointwise proof; what do Collatz researchers' heuristics (Tao's almost-all result via logarithmic density) suggest for ES?
connection: Tao (2019) proved almost all Collatz orbits attain almost bounded values via a 'logarithmic density + invariant measure' argument; ES has almost-all results via sieve. The Collatz pointwise question remains open for the same 'no reservoir' reason. Structural comparison: Collatz has a dynamical system; ES has none (no orbit) — see the orbit-absence lemma. So ES is 'Collatz without the map'.
why: Comparison sharpens what ES lacks (a map) and what it has (algebra: factorisations); a hybrid (define a map on certificates) is the 'Lyapunov function' item.
first_step: Read Tao's Collatz paper intro for the heuristic model and see if the 'Syracuse random variable' method has an ES analogue (random model of the factorisation of 4Cp+1 as C varies — the Kubilius model item).
refs: Tao, 'Almost all orbits of the Collatz map attain almost bounded values' (Forum Math Pi 2022)

title: Crowd computing: a BOINC/Folding-style project to extend ES verification to 10²⁰ AND collect the certificate census (which form fires first) as a public dataset
connection: Verification alone is of limited value, but a *structured* census (per prime: smallest C-form, smallest Type I d, smallest e-slice) at scale creates a dataset for pattern discovery and for testing the exceptional-set rate predictions.
why: Public datasets attract analysts; the compute is embarrassingly parallel.
first_step: Write the census kernel (fast C: trial division of 4Cp+1 for C ≤ 10³) and estimate throughput; publish the 10¹²-range dataset first.

title: Ask on the Lean Zulip (#maths) and Terence Tao's blog whether anyone has tried to formalise ES partial results or has unpublished ES notes
connection: Tao co-authored the key counting paper and writes about Erdős problems; the Zulip community has formalised Egyptian-fraction results (Bloom–Mehta). A short, specific question about the single-integer lower tail (FRONTIER §2) might get a comment from Tao or Bloom.
why: People lever; cheap.
first_step: Post a concise question in Zulip #maths (and as a comment on a relevant blog post) with the exact statement and the C-form exception data.

title: Compression of proofs: measure the description length of the 'certificate table' for all primes ≤ X as a function of X — the best possible 'proof length' of ES restricted to [1, X]
connection: If ES has no uniform proof, the shortest certificate table for primes ≤ X should grow like π(X)·(bits per certificate) with no compression; if a hidden uniform rule exists, compression beats this. Kolmogorov-style; measurable with real compressors on the sorted (p, C_min, a) table.
why: A direct, if crude, test for hidden uniformity, complementary to ML items.
first_step: Produce the table to 10⁷, compress with xz and with a specialised model (arithmetic coder conditioned on p mod 840); compare bits/prime to the entropy of C_min's empirical distribution.

title: Cellular automaton / tag system: encode the greedy-with-backtracking search for 3-term representations as a CA and study its space-time diagram for structure
connection: Rule-based searches sometimes reveal structure via their space-time diagrams (Wolfram's approach); the ES search tree over (x, y) with the two-term test is such a rule system.
why: Recreational/experimental; cheap; near-zero prior of a breakthrough but a possible visual hint.
first_step: Implement and plot for p ≤ 500; stop if nothing visible.
refs: Wolfram, A New Kind of Science

title: Finite differences in C: Δ_C of the indicator win(p, C) — is the sequence C ↦ win(p, C) 'eventually periodic' or 'quasi-periodic' for fixed p?
connection: For fixed p the C-form win indicator depends on the factorisation of the linear sequence 4Cp+1 — a shifted-prime-factor structure with no periodicity but with 'almost periodicity' in the Besicovitch sense (periodic in C mod q for each small prime q's contribution).
why: If win(p, ·) is Besicovitch almost periodic with a positive mean for every p, then infinitely many C win — pointwise ES with infinitude; the mean's positivity is the question, again — but almost-periodicity theory (Wintner, Schwarz–Spilker) gives a *formula* for the mean as a sum over 'Ramanujan expansions', which might be analysable.
first_step: Compute the Ramanujan–Fourier coefficients of win(p, C) over C ≤ 10⁵ for a few p; check whether the mean (the C-density of winning C) is approximated by the first few terms and is bounded away from 0 across p.

title: Density of winning C for fixed p: is lim inf_X (1/X)#{C ≤ X : win(p, C)} > 0, and is it a continuous function of p's local data?
connection: The expected win probability per C is ≈ τ(4Cp+1)/φ(4C)-ish which → 0 as C grows… so the natural density of winning C is 0; the right normalisation is log density or weights 1/C. Σ_{C ≤ X} win(p, C)/C ≈ c(p) log X? Then c(p) is 'the ES constant of p' and ES(p) ⟺ c(p) > 0 (plus finite checks). Is c(p) an Euler product in p's local data? Compute.
why: Defines a canonical real invariant c(p) whose positivity is ES(p) with infinitely many certificates; if c(p) has an Euler-product formula (plausible: heuristically it is Σ over C-structures of local densities) then ES(p) would follow from the product's positivity — the local factors are explicit and nonzero... the catch is convergence/rigour (this is M_BM at fixed p). Still, measuring c(p) numerically and fitting an Euler product is cheap.
first_step: For 50 primes, compute Σ_{C ≤ 10⁵} win(p, C)/C vs log X; extract c(p); regress log c(p) on Legendre symbols of small primes.

title: Umbral / generating-function identities for the count Σ_C x^C·#{a | 4Cp+1, a ≡ −1 (4C)}: Lambert-series structure
connection: Σ_N τ(N) x^N is a Lambert series; sums restricted to N = 4Cp+1 and a in a class tied to C are 'twisted Lambert series along an AP with varying modulus'. Lambert series have modular transformation properties; perhaps the C-form generating function has a transformation law relating p and 1/p-ish parameters.
why: A transformation law would be a rigid analytic structure (like Zagier's for Σ H(n)q^n). Low-to-medium prior.
first_step: Compute the generating function numerically for small p at |x| < 1 and test for simple transformation behaviour under x → e^{−2πt} ↦ t → 1/(p t)-type substitutions.

title: Wythoff/Fibonacci game lens: the pair (a, b) with ab = 4Cp+1, a ≡ b ≡ −1 mod 4C satisfies (a+1)(b+1) = 4C(p + u + v)…: write the Diophantine system as a lattice-point problem in the (u, v) plane under a hyperbola and count by Dirichlet's hyperbola method
connection: p = 4Cuv − u − v ⟺ (4Cu − 1)(4Cv − 1) = 4Cp + 1: for fixed C, solutions (u, v) are lattice points on a hyperbola; summing over C ≤ X, the total count is a 'hyperbola-method' sum Σ_C #{(u,v)}; Dirichlet's method gives main terms with error terms — standard for Σ_{C} τ(4Cp+1) — but here the hyperbola is in (u, v) with the constraint built in. Just the Type II count in the (u,v) coordinates: Σ_{C ≤ X} #{u ≤ v : (4Cu − 1) | 4Cp+1}.
why: Reorganising as 'u small' (u ≤ √(p/C)) vs 'u large' splits the count into a part with few divisors to check (u small ⟹ a = 4Cu − 1 small ⟹ trial division) and a symmetric part; the small-u part for ALL C ≤ X is a double sum Σ_C Σ_{u ≤ U} 1[(4Cu − 1) | 4Cp + 1] = Σ_C Σ_u 1[4Cp ≡ −1 mod (4Cu − 1)] = Σ_u Σ_C 1[p ≡ −(4C)^{−1} mod (4Cu − 1)] — for fixed u, as C varies the modulus 4Cu − 1 varies and the condition is p in a specific class mod it: for u = 1: a = 4C − 1, condition p ≡ −(4C)^{−1} ≡ −(1)^{−1}… 4C ≡ 1 mod a so (4C)^{−1} ≡ 1 and p ≡ −1 mod (4C − 1): u = 1 certificates ⟺ (4C − 1) | (p + 1) ⟺ p + 1 has a divisor ≡ 3 mod 4 — always true for p ≡ 1 mod 4? p + 1 ≡ 2 mod 4, (p+1)/2 odd; it has a divisor ≡ 3 mod 4 iff not all its prime factors are ≡ 1 mod 4. Nice: 'u = 1' identities = 'p + 1 has a prime factor ≡ 3 mod 4', a well-known ES case (it's an identity family? For a = 4C − 1 | p + 1 with p + 1 = a·k: this is Mordell's identity for p ≡ −1 mod a… indeed polynomial in p for each fixed a — the classical cover). Then u = 2: (8C − 1) | 4Cp + 1 ⟺ 4Cp ≡ −1 mod (8C − 1); 8C ≡ 1 ⟹ 4C ≡ 1/2 ⟹ p/2 ≡ −1 ⟹ p ≡ −2 mod (8C − 1): 'p + 2 has a divisor ≡ 7 mod 8'. u = 3: (12C − 1) | 4Cp + 1, 12C ≡ 1 ⟹ 4C ≡ 1/3 ⟹ p ≡ −3 mod (12C − 1): 'p + 3 has a divisor ≡ 11 mod 12'. In general: u-certificates ⟺ p + u has a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4u. (!!)

A clean reparametrisation: the C-form ⟺ ∃ u ≥ 1: p + u has a divisor ≡ −1 (mod 4u). This is the same shape (tied modulus) but with the *additive* shift p + u instead of the multiplicative 4Cp + 1 — i.e., the e-slice form with e = u (N = (p + e)/4-ish). It makes the role of u symmetric with v and shows the C-form is a statement about the divisors of p + 1, p + 2, p + 3, … in classes −1 mod 4, 8, 12, …: 'the shifted primes p + u, u = 1, 2, 3, …, cannot ALL avoid divisors ≡ −1 mod 4u'. Verify and record; this is probably the repo's e-slice form in disguise (seen).
first_step: Verify algebraically and numerically: C-form certificate ⟺ ∃u: (p + u) has a divisor a ≡ −1 (mod 4u) [with the cofactor condition automatically satisfied?]. Then for p = 409: p + u for u ≤ 60000 never has a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4u?! Check directly — this gives a very concrete statement about 409: '410, 411, 412, … have no divisor ≡ −1 mod 4, 8, 12, …' — e.g. 410 = 2·5·41: divisors ≡ 3 mod 4: none (5, 41 ≡ 1; 2·5 = 10 ≡ 2; …) ✓; 411 = 3·137: need ≡ 7 mod 8: 3, 137 ≡ 1, 411 ≡ 3 — none ✓; 412 = 4·103: need ≡ 11 mod 12: 103 ≡ 7, 206 ≡ 2, 412 ≡ 4 — none ✓ … So 409 is a prime such that p + u never has a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4u. A beautiful concrete puzzle.

title: The C-form as a statement about shifted primes: ES(p) ⟸ ∃u ≥ 1 with a divisor of p + u congruent to −1 (mod 4u) — compare with the theory of divisors of shifted primes (Erdős, Hooley's Δ-function, Ford's divisors in intervals)
connection: Given the reparametrisation (previous item), the C-form says: among p + 1, p + 2, …, some p + u has a divisor in the class −1 mod 4u. The divisor structure of shifted primes p + u (for fixed u, varying p) is classical (Erdős: p + 1 has typically log log p factors, the arcsine law holds for its divisors — Hall–Tenenbaum). The new twist: u varies with p fixed — the 'horizontal' direction again; Hooley's Δ-function and Ford's 'divisors in intervals' concern how divisors of a single integer are spread; here we need, for each u, a divisor of p + u near a specific residue class mod 4u — i.e., a divisor a with a ≡ −1 (4u); equivalently (a + 1)/4u ∈ ℤ, so a + 1 is a multiple of 4u while a divides p + u.
why: Reformulation puts ES into the well-developed 'divisors of shifted integers' literature (Hall–Tenenbaum 'Divisors'), with the familiar polylog count: E[#{u ≤ X : p + u has a divisor ≡ −1 (4u)}] ≈ Σ_u τ(p+u)/φ(4u) ≈ log p · log X. The pointwise question is identical but now 'horizontal in u' with additive shifts — the Hardy–Littlewood/Dickson flavour.
first_step: Verify the reparametrisation (bijection between (C, u, v) and (u, a)), then search Hall–Tenenbaum 'Divisors' for any theorem about divisors of n + u in a class depending on u (probably none); formulate the cleanest statement: 'for every non-square n ≥ 2 there is u ≥ 1 and a | n + u with a ≡ −1 (mod 4u)' — FALSE for n = 409 (if the C ≤ 60000 search transfers: u ≤ 60000).
refs: Ford, 'The distribution of integers with a divisor in a given interval' (Ann. Math 2008)

title: Type I in the shifted form: f | p² + 4c²d, f ≡ −p (mod 4cd) — is there an analogous 'p + u has a divisor in a class' statement for Type I (c = 1: f | p² + 4d, f ≡ −p mod 4d)?
connection: By analogy with the C-form reparametrisation, Type I c = 1 should be expressible as 'some pu + 1 (or p·u + something) has a divisor in a class'. From the e-slice form: Type I ↔ N = (pe + 1)/4 — multiplicative shift pe + 1; Type II ↔ N = (p + e)/4 — additive shift. So the two types are 'additive shifts p + e' and 'multiplicative shifts pe + 1' of p, each needing a divisor in a tied class. The C-form (p + u with divisor ≡ −1 mod 4u) is the additive one; Type I c=1 should be: pe + 1 has a divisor ≡ (something) mod 4e... Derive precisely.
why: A symmetric 'additive vs multiplicative shift' picture of the two types is a memorable organising principle, and the exceptions (409 fails additive; 2521 fails multiplicative) become 'a prime for which all additive shifts fail' vs 'all multiplicative shifts fail'. Both one-parameter statements are false for some primes; ES says the two never fail together (empirically).
first_step: Derive the Type I c=1 shifted statement from FRONTIER's e-slice form; verify numerically on 2521 (which e's fail and why); write the symmetric table.

title: Puzzle for people/MO: 'Show that for every prime p ≡ 1 (mod 4) EITHER some p + u has a divisor ≡ −1 (mod 4u) OR some pe + 1 has a divisor in its tied class' — the two-sided one-parameter statement as a self-contained elementary conjecture
connection: If the e-slice equivalence holds exactly (repo claims so), this two-sided statement IS ES for primes — but phrased with two one-parameter families of shifted integers, no x, y, z. The 409/2521 data show each side alone fails.
why: A maximally elementary, 'shifted-integer divisor' phrasing is the best bait for elementary number theorists and for olympiad-style insight; also a crisp statement for the Erdős problems site.
first_step: Pin down the exact tied class for the multiplicative side from the e-slice form; verify equivalence to ES for p ≤ 10⁴ by brute force; post.

title: Information from the literature on 'n + u has a divisor in a residue class mod u-dependent modulus' — search specifically for 'divisors of consecutive integers in prescribed classes' and 'Erdős problem on d | n + k with d ≡ ... mod k'
connection: The shifted reparametrisation suggests searching the Erdős problem corpus (erdosproblems.com has ~1000 problems) for anything about divisors of n + k in classes depending on k.
why: Erdős posed many 'consecutive integers' divisor problems; one may be ES-equivalent or ES-adjacent with known partial results.
first_step: Full-text search erdosproblems.com for 'divisor' + 'consecutive' / 'n+k'; read the hits.

title: Hasse-principle-style 'almost local' obstruction for 409 in the shifted form: is there a modulus M such that for every u the condition 'p + u has a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4u' is blocked by p's residue mod M? (A 'uniform local obstruction' — would contradict the belief that only squares are obstructed)
connection: For a fixed u the condition on p is a union of residue classes mod lcm-ish(4u·a); an obstruction for ALL u from a single residue p mod M would mean the C-form fails on an entire AP of primes — plausibly false (Dirichlet + the almost-all results for the C-form). So 409's failure is not an AP obstruction; is it then 'random' (and the C ≤ 60000 search just unlucky — implausible given the expected count Σ_{C ≤ 60000} τ(4·409C+1)/φ(4C) ≈ 52 wins) or a non-AP structural obstruction (like T1, which is a 'square' obstruction — not an AP either)? Expected 66 wins vs 0 observed strongly indicates an obstruction of a new type (not AP, not square).
why: The expected-count argument (≈ 52 expected certificates for 409 with C ≤ 60000 (computed: Σ τ(4·409·C+1)/φ(4C) = 51.8), zero observed) is the sharpest evidence that 409 is structurally obstructed in the C-form; identifying the obstruction type is a genuinely new piece of ES structure.
first_step: Compute the expected count Σ_{C ≤ 60000} τ(4·409·C + 1)/φ(4C) precisely (it is the natural heuristic) and compare with the 0 observed; then test the natural candidate obstruction: for 409, is the forced QNR condition (a/409) = −1 incompatible with a ≡ −1 (mod 4C) and a | 4·409C + 1 for a reason involving 409 ≡ 9 (mod 16) or 409's Gaussian representation 20² + 3²?

title: Exceptional primes vs the 'u = 1, 2, 3 classical identities': 409 + 1 = 410 = 2·5·41 (all odd factors ≡ 1 mod 4), 411 = 3·137 (3 ≡ 3 mod 8, 137 ≡ 1), 412 = 4·103 … — build the 'residue avoidance table' for p + u, u ≤ 50, for 409 and for a random control
connection: A table showing, for each u, the prime factors of p + u mod 4u and why no subset product is ≡ −1 — the 'forensics' item in the additive form, where it is readable by hand.
why: Hand-readable evidence is the fastest route to a conjecture about the obstruction type.
first_step: Generate the table; look for the pattern (e.g., 'every odd prime factor q of p + u satisfies (q/409) = +1 or q ≡ 1 mod 4u' — a Legendre-symbol coincidence pattern).

title: Hypothesis: 409 is obstructed because every divisor a of p + u with a ≡ −1 (mod 4u) must satisfy (a/p) = −1 AND a ≡ −u^{-1}·... — derive the second forced symbol in the shifted form
connection: In the shifted form a | p + u ⟹ p ≡ −u (mod a) ⟹ (p/a) = (−u/a) = (−1/a)(u/a) = −(u/a) (a ≡ 3 mod 4); also a ≡ −1 (mod 4u) ⟹ (u/a) = +1 by reciprocity (as before for C) ⟹ (p/a) = −1 ⟹ (a/p) = −1. Same forced symbol. Now also consider (u/p): from a | p + u, nothing forces (u/p). Hmm; but the cofactor b = (p+u)/a satisfies... In the C-form, the cofactor was ≡ −1 mod 4C too; in the shifted form the cofactor b = (p + u)/a — its class mod 4u? p + u ≡ ? mod 4u: p ≡ 1 mod 4, so p + u mod 4u is p + u — not controlled. So in the shifted form the cofactor is unconstrained — then the (u, a) ↔ (C, a, b) bijection must impose b ≡ ... let me recheck: from 4Cp + 1 = ab, a = 4Cu − 1: b = (4Cp + 1)/(4Cu − 1); with the claim 'a | p + u': 4Cp + 1 ≡ 0 (mod a) and 4Cu ≡ 1 (mod a) ⟹ 4Cp ≡ −1 ⟹ multiply by u: 4Cu·p ≡ −u ⟹ p ≡ −u (mod a) ✓. Conversely a | p + u with a ≡ −1 (mod 4u): set 4Cu = a + 1 (C = (a+1)/(4u) ∈ ℤ ✓), then 4Cp = (a+1)p/u ≡ ? We need a | 4Cp + 1: 4Cp + 1 = ((a+1)p + u)/u; mod a: (p + u)/u ≡ 0 ✓ (since a | p + u and gcd(a, u) = 1 as a ≡ −1 mod u). So b = (4Cp+1)/a is an integer and b ≡ ? mod 4C: ab = 4Cp + 1 ≡ 1, a ≡ −1 ⟹ b ≡ −1 ✓ automatically. Good: the bijection holds with no extra condition. So the shifted form is exactly right: C-form ⟺ ∃u: (p + u) has a divisor ≡ −1 (mod 4u).
why: Confirms the reparametrisation rigorously (no hidden cofactor condition) and shows the only forced symbol is (a/p) = −1; so 409's obstruction, if structural, is not a second Jacobi symbol of this simple type — it must involve the interplay of a ≡ −1 (4u), a | 409 + u across u.
first_step: Record the proof; then compute for 409 the set of 'near misses': u ≤ 10⁴ and divisors a of 409 + u with a ≡ −1 mod 4u′ for the largest u′ | u-ish — see how close the condition comes to being satisfied.

title: Shifted form for composite n and the T1 reproof: m² + u has a divisor ≡ −1 (mod 4u) is impossible — one-line check via (a/m²) = 1
connection: For n = m²: a | m² + u, a ≡ −1 (mod 4u) ⟹ (a/m²) = 1 but the forced symbol says (a/n) = −1 — contradiction. T1 for the C-form in the shifted language is immediate. For general n the forced symbol is (a/n) = −1 (Jacobi), which for n = 409·k² etc. reduces to (a/409) = −1 — so the shifted-form exceptional set is closed under multiplication by odd squares coprime to… (need also a | n + u to be consistent) — test numerically whether 409·9 is an exception.
why: Closure under square multiples would give an infinite non-square family of C-form exceptions (409m²), making the C-form exceptional set 'squares ∪ square-multiples of sporadic ∪ ?' — a rich structure to compare with the U(n) sporadics {105, 2961, 3985, 25305, 111969, 978145} (are these square multiples of smaller ones? 2961 = 9·329 = 9·7·47; 25305 = 105·241; hmm).
first_step: Compute the C-form exceptional set for n ≤ 10⁵ (all n ≡ 1 mod 4, u ≤ 5000) and test closure under n ↦ nm²; compare to the U(n) list.

title: Heuristic repair: the expected-count heuristic for the C-form must be corrected by the forced QNR condition — only divisors a with (a/p) = −1 count, halving the expectation; and if a second hidden constraint exists it halves again — is 409's zero count explainable by a cascade of such 'free' constraints?
connection: Each forced symbol halves the expected count; the observed 0 for 409 at expected ≈ 52 (or 26 after QNR) would need ~5–6 independent forced constraints. Alternatively, a single structural obstruction. Determine which by finding the forced-symbol set empirically: for all C-form certificates (over many p), tabulate the joint distribution of (a/q) for small q, a mod 16, etc., and see which symbols are forced (always equal) vs free.
why: Systematic discovery of forced constraints on certificates is a well-defined computation and could reveal the complete 'reciprocity signature' of the C-form, of which (a/p) = −1 is the first element.
first_step: Collect ~10⁵ certificates (p ≤ 10⁵, C ≤ 200); for each candidate symbol s(a, p, C) in a list of ~50 (Jacobi symbols, residues mod small powers of 2, Kronecker symbols (a/2), (−1/a), (p/u)...), compute entropy of its distribution; list zero-entropy ones.

title: Mutual exclusion of the two exceptional sets (C-form vs Type I c=1): is there a proof that no prime can be in both? That would be ES for primes via two one-parameter families
connection: Data: {409, 577, 5569, 9601} ∩ {2521} = ∅ below 20000. If 'p fails the additive form' forces a structural property (e.g. a certain Jacobi signature) that is incompatible with 'p fails the multiplicative form', then ES(p) would follow from their disjointness. This is a precise conjecture (stronger than ES) that is testable to large ranges and might be approachable by reciprocity (both failure conditions are reciprocity-flavoured).
why: Turns ES into the disjointness of two explicitly characterised (conjecturally thin) sets — a shape amenable to 'if both fail then (symbol) = +1 and = −1' arguments if the failures have forced signatures.
first_step: Extend both exceptional sets to 10⁶ (cheap in Pari); if still disjoint, look for a forced signature of each failure type (e.g. additive failure ⟹ p ≡ 1 mod 8? multiplicative failure ⟹ p ≡ 1 mod 840?).

title: Meta: hand the C-form/Type I c=1 exceptional-set program to a dedicated lane — it is cheap, concrete, and produces test cases regardless of outcome
connection: The program: (i) census to 10⁶–10⁷ of both one-parameter exceptional sets; (ii) forced-symbol discovery; (iii) obstruction proofs for 409 and 2521; (iv) disjointness conjecture; (v) OEIS + MO publication.
why: Of all items in this lane these have the best ratio of concreteness to novelty; the outcome calibrates the whole 'one-parameter vs two-parameter' question.
first_step: Write a one-page brief for a follow-up lane with the five steps and the scripts to start from.
